interviewQuestions.question: Compare direct-mapped, set-associative, and fully associative caches. Why do real CPUs use set-associative?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Direct-mapped placement gives each block exactly one possible slot, determined by its index bits. It's the cheapest hardware — one tag comparator, one lookup — but two blocks that happen to map to the same slot will thrash each other out even if the rest of the cache sits idle, so it's prone to conflict misses that have nothing to do with total working-set size.

Fully associative placement lets a block go into *any* slot, so there's never a placement collision — a block is only evicted by a genuine capacity limit, never by an unlucky index. The cost is a comparator per slot checked in parallel on every lookup, which is fine for a 16-64 entry structure like a TLB but doesn't scale to a multi-thousand-line L2 or L3 — the comparator count and the wiring to broadcast the tag to all of them would dominate the chip.

Set-associative placement is the middle ground real caches actually use: an address's index bits pick one set, and within that set the block can go into any of N ways. That bounds the comparator count to N per set instead of one per entire cache, dramatically cheaper than fully associative, while still absorbing most of the collisions a direct-mapped design would suffer, because N blocks can now coexist at the same index. This is why nearly every L1/L2/L3 you'll encounter is quoted as 4-way, 8-way, or 16-way — it's the sweet spot between direct-mapped's collision problem and fully-associative's hardware cost.

**Testing:** whether you can explain *why* the middle ground wins on cost and collision-resistance together, not just name the three schemes.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Placement schemes compared

interviewQuestions.question: Given a 32 KB, 8-way set-associative L1 with 64-byte lines, how would you compute the index and tag for a given address?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First get the geometry: total lines = 32KB / 64B = 512 lines; with 8 ways, that's 512/8 = 64 sets. The block offset needs `log2(64) = 6` bits (bytes within a line). The set index needs `log2(64) = 6` bits (which of the 64 sets). Everything above those 12 bits is the tag.

So for a 32-bit address, I'd split it as: bits [31:12] = tag (20 bits), bits [11:6] = set index (6 bits), bits [5:0] = block offset (6 bits). To look up an address: take bits [11:6], go to that set, compare the address's tag bits [31:12] against the tag stored in each of the 8 ways in that set in parallel — a hit is any way whose stored tag matches and whose valid bit is set.

A worked example: address `0x00012345` in binary is `... 0001 0010 0011 0100 0101`. Offset = last 6 bits = `000101` = 5 (byte 5 within the line). Index = next 6 bits — you'd extract bits [11:6] directly from the hex value (`0x345 >> 6 & 0x3F`) rather than redo the binary by hand in an interview, but the mechanism is the same: shift right by the offset width, mask to the index width. Everything left of that is the tag that gets stored and compared.

The interview trap here is off-by-one on bit widths — always derive them from the geometry (`log2(sets)` and `log2(line size)`) rather than guessing, and always compute sets as total lines / associativity, not total lines directly.

**Testing:** whether you can derive index/offset/tag widths from cache geometry mechanically, without memorizing a specific example.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Computing index and tag

interviewQuestions.question: You're designing a cache and associativity is expensive in your power budget. What are the real costs of going lower-associativity, and how would you mitigate them?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Higher associativity costs power and area in two places: the parallel tag comparison (N comparators activated on every access, each one doing a full tag-width XOR/compare) and the wider multiplexer needed to select the hit way's data out of N candidates. Both scale roughly linearly with associativity, and comparators are switched on every single access whether it hits or misses, so this is a genuinely recurring power cost, not a one-time area cost.

Going lower-associativity (say 8-way down to 4-way, or 4-way down to direct-mapped) saves that power and area but reintroduces conflict misses for access patterns that happen to alias into the same set — and the miss penalty of going to the next level down usually costs far more energy (and cycles) than the comparator power it saved, so the trade-off isn't free just because it looks cheaper on the tag-compare line item.

Mitigations that keep most of the miss-rate benefit at lower hardware cost: skewed-associative caches (using a different hash per way so pathological strides don't alias identically across all ways), way prediction (guess the likely way from history and only activate that comparator, falling back to full comparison on a misprediction), and victim caches (a small fully-associative buffer that catches lines just evicted by conflict misses, cheap because it's tiny). These recover much of full-associativity's collision resistance without paying full associativity's per-access comparator cost on every lookup.

**Testing:** whether you understand associativity's cost is a genuine per-access power cost, and know real mitigations beyond "just add more ways."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Associativity's real cost
